questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Two stars, A and B, have the same density but star A has twice the radius of star B.

What is the ratio of the gravitational field strength at the surface of star A to that at the surface of star B?
questions.stemText: Two stars, A and B, have the same density but star A has twice the radius of star B. What is the ratio of the gravitational field strength at the surface of star A to that at the surface of star B? A 1 : 4 B 1 : 2 C 2 : 1 D 8 : 1

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Must express mass in terms of density and radius before applying g = GM/r².
questions.misconception: Ignoring that the larger star also has more mass

explanation.body:
$g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$ and $M = \rho\left(\tfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3\right)$, so $g = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi G\rho R$.

With the same density, $g \propto R$, so $g_A : g_B = 2 : 1$.

perOption.A: Uses $g \propto 1/R^2$ with the same mass, but the mass is not the same.
perOption.B: Inverts the ratio.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the mass ratio ($M \propto R^3$) and forgets the $1/R^2$ factor.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A satellite of mass $6.9\times10^{2}$ kg orbits the Earth in a circular orbit of radius $6.5\times10^{6}$ m. Its orbital speed is $7.9\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. A rocket engine is fired such that the satellite moves into a higher orbit of radius $7.2\times10^{6}$ m where its orbital speed decreases to $7.5\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. Which statement about the change in total energy of the satellite is correct? Mass of the Earth $= 6.0\times10^{24}$ kg. A The satellite gains approximately $2\times10^{9}$ J. B The satellite gains approximately $4\times10^{9}$ J. C The satellite loses approximately $2\times10^{9}$ J. D The satellite loses approximately $6\times10^{9}$ J.

stemImage.alt: Question 9: A satellite of mass 6.9  102 kg orbits the Earth in a circular orbit of radius 6.5  106 m. Its orbital speed is 7.9 km s–1. A rocket engine is fired such that

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs total orbital energy (KE + GPE) at both radii and careful handling of signs and small differences.
questions.misconception: Thinking that a slower satellite has lost energy, or using only KE or only GPE

explanation.body:
Total energy in orbit is $-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$, so

$\Delta TE = -\dfrac{(6.67\times10^{-11})(6.0\times10^{24})(690)}{2}\left[\dfrac{1}{7.2\times10^{6}} - \dfrac{1}{6.5\times10^{6}}\right] = +2\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{J}$.

Or: $\Delta KE = \tfrac{1}{2}(690)[(7.5\times10^{3})^2 - (7.9\times10^{3})^2] = -2.13\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{J}$ and $\Delta GPE = -GMm\left[\dfrac{1}{7.2\times10^{6}} - \dfrac{1}{6.5\times10^{6}}\right] = +4.13\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{J}$, giving $\Delta TE = +2\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The satellite gains total energy moving to a higher orbit.
perOption.B: This is only the gain in GPE; it ignores the loss of KE.
perOption.C: This is only the change in KE; the GPE gain is larger.
perOption.D: Treats both the KE and GPE changes as losses ($-2.1 - 4.1 \approx -6\times10^{9}$ J).

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Two isolated point masses, P of mass $m$ and Q of mass $2m$, are separated by a distance $3d$. X is a point a distance $d$ from P and $2d$ from Q. [Diagram: P on the left, X at distance $d$ to its right, Q at distance $2d$ further right, all on one line.] What is the net gravitational field strength and the net gravitational potential at X? (field strength; potential) A $0$; $-\dfrac{Gm}{d}$ B $\dfrac{Gm}{d^2}$; $-2\dfrac{Gm}{d}$ C $0$; $-3\dfrac{Gm}{d}$ D $\dfrac{Gm}{2d^2}$; $-2\dfrac{Gm}{d}$

stemImage.alt: Question 10: Two isolated point masses, P of mass m and Q of mass 2m, are separated by a distance 3d. X is a point a distance d from P and 2d from Q. What is the net gravita

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Vector addition of fields in opposite directions plus scalar addition of potentials.
questions.misconception: Treating field strength as a scalar sum or potential as a vector that cancels

explanation.body: At X the fields point in opposite directions, each towards its source mass. Their magnitudes are $g_P=Gm/d^2$ and $g_Q=G(2m)/(2d)^2=Gm/(2d^2)$, so the net field is $Gm/(2d^2)$ towards P. Gravitational potential is scalar, so $\phi=-Gm/d-G(2m)/(2d)=-2Gm/d$.

perOption.A: Assumes the fields cancel and counts only one potential contribution.
perOption.B: Gives the correct potential but counts only P’s field.
perOption.C: Assumes the fields cancel and overlooks that Q is twice as far from X as P.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: The diagram shows four equipotential lines in a gravitational field. Which arrow (A, B, C or D) shows the direction of the gravitational field strength at point X? [Diagram: four curved dashed equipotential lines labelled from top to bottom $-500$, $-400$, $-300$, $-200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$. At point X on the $-300$ line, arrow A points up (perpendicular, towards $-500$), arrow C points down (towards $-200$), arrows B and D point right and left along the equipotential.]

stemImage.alt: Question 11: The diagram shows four equipotential lines in a gravitational field. Which arrow (A, B, C or D) shows the direction of the gravitational field strength at point

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires knowing field lines are perpendicular to equipotentials and point to lower potential.
questions.misconception: Thinking the field points towards higher (less negative) potential

explanation.body: The gravitational field is perpendicular to the equipotential through X, leaving A and C as candidates. Since $g=-\mathrm d\phi/\mathrm dx$ along the normal, the field points toward decreasing potential, from $-300$ toward $-400\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Points along the tangent to the equipotential through X.
perOption.C: Points toward increasing gravitational potential.
perOption.D: Points along the tangent to the equipotential through X.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Two points P and Q are a fixed distance apart on a line joining them to an object considered as a point mass. Point P is at a distance $x$ away from the object. The magnitude of the gravitational potential at point P is $\phi$. [Diagram: object on the left, P at distance $x$, Q further along the same line.] The two points move away from the object, along the line, maintaining their fixed separation such that point P is now at a distance $2x$ away from the object. What happens to the magnitude of the gravitational potential at the new point P and to the magnitude of the gravitational potential difference between point P and point Q? [Table: magnitude of potential at new P / magnitude of p.d.] A: less than $\phi/2$, decreases. B: less than $\phi/2$, stays the same. C: $\phi/2$, decreases. D: $\phi/2$, stays the same.

stemImage.alt: Question 12: Two points P and Q are a fixed distance apart on a line joining them to an object considered as a point mass. Point P is at a distance, x away from the object.

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Uses φ ∝ 1/r and the fact that the field weakens with distance.
questions.misconception: Thinking potential difference stays the same for a fixed separation, as in a uniform field

explanation.body: The potential is $-GM/r$, so doubling P's distance halves the potential magnitude to $\phi/2$. The inverse-distance curve is steeper nearer the mass, so moving P and Q outward by the same distance reduces the potential magnitude at P by more than at Q. The magnitude of the potential difference therefore decreases.

perOption.A: Reduces P's potential magnitude by too much for a doubling of distance.
perOption.B: Reduces P's potential magnitude by too much and assumes P and Q change by equal amounts.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Assumes equal outward shifts cause equal potential changes.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Three planets, X, Y and Z have masses M, M and 2M respectively, are arranged in a triangle and are equidistant from each other. [Diagram: equilateral triangle with X at top, Y bottom-left, Z bottom-right; O at the centre, distance r from each planet.] What is the magnitude and direction of the gravitational field strength at point O? (magnitude, direction) A 0, no direction B $\frac{GM}{r^2}$, towards X C $\frac{GM}{r^2}$, towards Z D $\frac{G(2M - \sqrt{3}M)}{r^2}$, towards Z

stemImage.alt: Question 8: Use the following diagram to answer questions 8 and 9. Three planets, X, Y and Z have masses M, M and 2M respectively, are arranged in a triangle and are equidi

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Vector addition of three point-mass fields at the centroid of an equilateral triangle.
questions.misconception: Combining two fields at 120° as if they were at 60° (getting $\sqrt{3}$)

explanation.body: The key takes $g_X=g_Y=GM/r^2$ and $g_Z=2GM/r^2$. It resolves the fields of X and Y along the line through O and Z, using $30^\circ$ for each angle, so their components perpendicular to that line cancel and their components away from Z sum to $2(GM/r^2)\cos30^\circ=\sqrt{3}GM/r^2$. Subtracting this from Z’s field gives the key’s result, $G(2M-\sqrt{3}M)/r^2$ towards Z.

perOption.A: Treats the three fields as cancelling despite Z having twice the mass of X or Y.
perOption.B: Points the resultant towards X even though the additional mass is at Z.
perOption.C: This is the physical result at the centre, where the three equal-mass contributions cancel and the extra mass at Z supplies the net field.
perOption.D: Correct according to the key’s component calculation.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Three planets, X, Y and Z have masses M, M and 2M respectively, are arranged in a triangle and are equidistant from each other. [Diagram: equilateral triangle with X at top, Y bottom-left, Z bottom-right; O at the centre, distance r from each planet.] What is the gravitational potential at O and its direction? (potential, direction) A 0, no direction B $-\frac{GM}{r}$, towards Z C $\frac{GM}{r}$, towards Z D $-\frac{4GM}{r}$, no direction

stemImage.alt: Question 9: Use the following diagram to answer questions 8 and 9. Three planets, X, Y and Z have masses M, M and 2M respectively, are arranged in a triangle and are equidi

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Scalar sum of potentials plus recognising potential has no direction.
questions.misconception: Treating potential as a vector

explanation.body: Gravitational potential is a scalar, so add the three contributions at O directly. This gives $\phi=-GM/r-GM/r-G(2M)/r=-4GM/r$. The potential has no direction.

perOption.A: Treats the three negative potentials as if they could cancel by symmetry.
perOption.B: Uses a single mass-M contribution and assigns a direction to a scalar.
perOption.C: Uses the wrong sign and assigns a direction to a scalar.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A satellite is in a stable circular orbit around Earth. Due to a brief atmospheric drag, it loses energy and transitions into a new, stable circular orbit with a smaller radius.

Which statement about the satellite is true?
questions.stemText: A satellite is in a stable circular orbit around Earth. Due to a brief atmospheric drag, it loses energy and transitions into a new, stable circular orbit with a smaller radius. Which statement about the satellite is true? A The linear speed increases, and the orbital period decreases. B The linear speed decreases, and the gravitational force decreases. C The kinetic energy decreases, and the potential energy increases. D The total mechanical energy remains constant, and the period increases.

options.label: A
options.text: The linear speed increases, and the orbital period decreases.

options.label: B
options.text: The linear speed decreases, and the gravitational force decreases.

options.label: C
options.text: The kinetic energy decreases, and the potential energy increases.

options.label: D
options.text: The total mechanical energy remains constant, and the period increases.

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Counter-intuitive result that losing energy increases orbital speed.
questions.misconception: Assuming that losing energy to drag makes the satellite slower

explanation.body: Gravity supplies the centripetal force, so $GMm/r^2=mv^2/r$ and $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$. The speed therefore increases as the orbital radius decreases. The period $T=2\pi r/v=2\pi\sqrt{r^3/(GM)}$ decreases because the orbit is shorter and the satellite travels faster.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Both orbital speed and gravitational force increase at the smaller radius.
perOption.C: Kinetic energy increases and gravitational potential energy decreases.
perOption.D: Both total mechanical energy and orbital period decrease.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: At the surface of the Earth, the gravitational field strength is $g$, and the gravitational potential is $\phi$. The radius of the Earth is $R$. An object, whose weight on the surface of the Earth is $W$, is moved to a height $3R$ above the surface. What are the weight of the object and the gravitational potential at this height? (weight, potential) A $W/16$, $\phi/4$ B $W/16$, $\phi/3$ C $W/4$, $\phi/4$ D $W/4$, $\phi/3$

stemImage.alt: Question 10: At the surface of the Earth, the gravitational field strength is g, and the gravitational potential is . The radius of the Earth is R. An object, whose weight

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Ratio reasoning with $g \propto 1/r^2$ and $\phi \propto 1/r$, with the height-vs-distance trap.
questions.misconception: Using height above the surface (3R) instead of distance from Earth's centre (4R)

explanation.body: At Earth’s surface, $W=GMm/R^2$ and $\phi=-GM/R$. At height $3R$, the distance from Earth’s centre is $4R$. Thus $W'=GMm/(4R)^2=W/16$ and $\phi'=-GM/(4R)=\phi/4$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses the height above the surface as the distance for the potential.
perOption.C: Scales weight with inverse distance instead of inverse distance squared.
perOption.D: Uses inverse-distance scaling for weight and uses the height above the surface for the potential.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A satellite has a weight of $W$ on the surface of the Earth. What is the weight of the satellite when it is in a circular orbit at a height of $5R$ above the surface of the Earth, where $R$ is the radius of the earth? A $\dfrac{W}{36}$ B $\dfrac{W}{25}$ C $\dfrac{W}{5}$ D 0

stemImage.alt: Question 9: A satellite has a weight of W on the surface of the Earth. What is the weight of the satellite when it is in a circular orbit at a height of 5R above the surfac

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Inverse-square ratio, with the trap of using height rather than distance from the centre.
questions.misconception: Using height above the surface instead of distance from the centre, or thinking orbiting objects are weightless

explanation.body: At Earth’s surface the satellite’s weight is $W=GMm/R^2$. Its orbit is at a distance $R+5R=6R$ from Earth’s centre. There its weight is $GMm/(6R)^2=W/36$.

perOption.A: Correct. The centre-to-satellite distance is six Earth radii.
perOption.B: This uses the altitude as the distance from Earth’s centre.
perOption.C: This uses the altitude as the orbital radius and assumes an inverse-linear dependence.
perOption.D: Orbital free fall gives zero apparent weight, while gravity still supplies the centripetal force.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Two satellites P and Q orbit the Earth due to the gravitational field of the Earth. P and Q are at distances R and 3R from the Earth’s surface respectively, where R is the radius of the earth.

The speed of Q is v.

What is the speed of P?
questions.stemText: Two satellites P and Q orbit the Earth due to the gravitational field of the Earth. P and Q are at distances R and 3R from the Earth’s surface respectively, where R is the radius of the earth. The speed of Q is v. What is the speed of P? A  B  C  D

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Ratio of orbital speeds; main trap is measuring distance from the surface instead of the centre.
questions.misconception: Using distance from Earth's surface instead of from its centre

explanation.body: The orbital radii measured from Earth's centre are $2R$ for P and $4R$ for Q. Gravity supplies the centripetal force, so $mv^2/r=GMm/r^2$ and orbital speed is proportional to $1/\sqrt r$. Hence $v_P/v_Q=\sqrt{4R/(2R)}=\sqrt2$ and $v_P=\sqrt2\,v$.

perOption.A: Uses the surface altitudes as radii and makes the inner satellite slower.
perOption.B: Inverts the orbital-radius ratio for the two speeds.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the surface altitudes $R$ and $3R$ as orbital radii.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The Moon has a diameter that is approximately 0.25 times the diameter of the Earth, and the mass of Moon is 0.012 times the mass of the Earth.

Given that the gravitational potential at the Earth’s surface is ‒63 MJ $\mathrm{kg}^{‒1}$.

What is an approximate value for the gravitational potential at the surface of Moon?
questions.stemText: The Moon has a diameter that is approximately 0.25 times the diameter of the Earth, and the mass of Moon is 0.012 times the mass of the Earth. Given that the gravitational potential at the Earth’s surface is ‒63 MJ kg‒1. What is an approximate value for the gravitational potential at the surface of Moon? A ‒0.19 MJ $\mathrm{kg}^{‒1}$ B ‒3.0 MJ $\mathrm{kg}^{‒1}$ C ‒12 MJ $\mathrm{kg}^{‒1}$ D ‒1300 MJ $\mathrm{kg}^{‒1}$

options.label: A
options.text: ‒0.19 MJ $\mathrm{kg}^{‒1}$

options.label: B
options.text: ‒3.0 MJ $\mathrm{kg}^{‒1}$

options.label: C
options.text: ‒12 MJ $\mathrm{kg}^{‒1}$

options.label: D
options.text: ‒1300 MJ $\mathrm{kg}^{‒1}$

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Single ratio using $\phi = -GM/r$.
questions.misconception: Using an inverse-square dependence on radius for potential

explanation.body: Gravitational potential at the surface is $\phi=-GM/r$. The Moon’s radius is $0.25$ times Earth’s radius, the same ratio as for the diameters. Thus $\phi_M=(0.012/0.25)(-63)\approx-3.0\ \mathrm{MJ\,kg^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Multiplies by the radius ratio although potential varies inversely with radius.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses an inverse-square dependence appropriate to gravitational field strength.
perOption.D: Inverts the ratio of the Moon’s potential to Earth’s potential.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A planet orbits around a star with a period of T and an orbiting radius of r. The planet is then hit by some asteroids, causing its total energy to decrease and its orbital radius to decrease to 0.25r.

In this new orbit, how many revolutions does the planet make in the same time T?
questions.stemText: A planet orbits around a star with a period of T and an orbiting radius of r. The planet is then hit by some asteroids, causing its total energy to decrease and its orbital radius to decrease to 0.25r. In this new orbit, how many revolutions does the planet make in the same time T? A 0.13 B 0.25 C 4.0 D 8.0

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Direct use of Kepler's third law with a ratio.
questions.misconception: Assuming period is proportional to radius

explanation.body: Gravity supplies the centripetal force, so $GMm/r^2=mr(2\pi/T)^2$ and $T^2=4\pi^2r^3/(GM)$. For the original and new periods, $T^2/T_2^2=r^3/(0.25r)^3=64$. Thus $T=8T_2$, and the planet completes eight revolutions in time $T$.

perOption.A: Gives the new period as a fraction of the original period instead of the number of revolutions.
perOption.B: Uses the radius ratio as the number of revolutions.
perOption.C: Assumes the period is directly proportional to radius.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: Which statement about geostationary orbits on Earth is false?
questions.stemText: Which statement about geostationary orbits on Earth is false? A A geostationary orbit must be directly above the equator. B All satellites in geostationary orbit must have the same mass. C The period of a geostationary orbit must be 24 hours. D There is only one possible radius for a geostationary orbit.

options.label: A
options.text: A geostationary orbit must be directly above the equator.

options.label: B
options.text: All satellites in geostationary orbit must have the same mass.

options.label: C
options.text: The period of a geostationary orbit must be 24 hours.

options.label: D
options.text: There is only one possible radius for a geostationary orbit.

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Direct recall of the defining features of a geostationary orbit.
questions.misconception: Thinking orbital radius depends on the satellite's mass

explanation.body: Gravity provides the centripetal force, so $\frac{GMm}{r^2}=mr(2\pi/T)^2$. This gives $T^2=\frac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3$, which is independent of the satellite’s mass. The claim that all such satellites must have the same mass is false.

perOption.A: A geostationary orbit lies in the equatorial plane so the satellite stays above one point on the equator.
perOption.B: Correct. The satellite’s mass cancels.
perOption.C: The orbital period must match Earth’s rotation period, about 24 hours.
perOption.D: The required period fixes a unique radius because $T^2\propto r^3$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The centres of two isolated stars with masses $M$ and $4M$ are separated by a fixed distance $d$.

[Diagram: a small star of mass $M$ on the left and a larger star of mass $4M$ on the right; the distance between their centres is labelled $d$.]

At what distance from the centre of the star of mass $M$ is the resultant gravitational field strength equal to zero?

A $\dfrac{d}{5}$   B $\dfrac{d}{3}$   C $\dfrac{d}{2}$   D $\dfrac{2d}{3}$

stemImage.alt: Question 10: The centres of two isolated stars with masses M and 4M are separated by a fixed distance d. 4M M d At what distance from the centre of the star of mass M is the

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: A standard null-point problem with a simple square root.
questions.misconception: Forgetting to take the square root of the mass ratio

explanation.body:
The resultant field is zero where the two field strengths are equal. Let $x$ be the distance from the star of mass $M$:

$\dfrac{GM}{x^2} = \dfrac{G(4M)}{(d - x)^2} \Rightarrow \dfrac{(d - x)^2}{x^2} = 4 \Rightarrow \dfrac{d - x}{x} = 2$

$x = \dfrac{d}{3}$

perOption.A: Uses the mass ratio 4 directly for the distance ratio, forgetting the square in the inverse square law.
perOption.B: Correct. The distance ratio is $\sqrt{4} = 2$.
perOption.C: Takes the midpoint, which would only be correct for equal masses.
perOption.D: Gives the distance from the larger star, $4M$, instead of from $M$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A planet has mass $M$ and radius $R$.

An object of mass $m$ is moved by means of an external force from the surface of the planet to $3R$ from the centre of the planet.

What is the work done on the object by the external force?

A $-\dfrac{2GMm}{3R}$   B $-\dfrac{4GMm}{3R}$   C $\dfrac{2GMm}{3R}$   D $\dfrac{4GMm}{3R}$

stemImage.alt: Question 11: A planet has mass M and radius R. An object of mass m is moved by means of an external force from the surface of the planet to 3R from the centre of the planet.

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: A direct use of $\phi = -GM/r$, but sign handling trips up some students.
questions.misconception: Sign errors when subtracting negative potentials

explanation.body:
Work done by the external force $= m\,\Delta\phi$:

$W = m\left[\left(-\dfrac{GM}{3R}\right) - \left(-\dfrac{GM}{R}\right)\right] = \dfrac{2GMm}{3R}$

perOption.A: Has the right magnitude but the wrong sign: work must be done on the object to raise its potential.
perOption.B: Adds the magnitudes of the two potentials instead of taking their difference, and has the wrong sign.
perOption.C: Correct. $W = m(\phi_f - \phi_i)$.
perOption.D: Adds the magnitudes of the two potentials instead of taking their difference.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The moon orbits the Earth once every 27.3 days, with a mean orbital radius of $R$. The period of an Earth satellite with an orbital radius of $\frac{R}{30}$ is

A  0.17 hours
B  4.0 hours
C  68 hours
D  260 hours

stemImage.alt: Question 13: The moon orbits the Earth once every 27.3 days, with a mean orbital radius of R. The R is period of an Earth satellite with an orbital radius of 30

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Use the orbital period–radius scaling and convert days to hours.
questions.misconception: Using the wrong power of orbital radius

explanation.body: For orbits around Earth, $T^2\propto R^3$. With the satellite period $T$ in days, $(27.3/T)^2=[R/(R/30)]^3$, so $T=0.166\ \mathrm{day}\approx4.0\ \mathrm{hours}$.

perOption.A: This is approximately the period in days, reported as hours.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: This corresponds to reducing the period by only about a factor of 10, whereas the orbital radius change requires a factor of $30^{3/2}$.
perOption.D: This gives too long a period for a radius reduced by a factor of 30, since the period scales as radius to the power $3/2$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A stationary object is released from a point at a height of 2R from the surface of the Moon which has radius R and mass M.

What is the correct expression for the speed of the object on hitting the Moon?
questions.stemText: A stationary object is released from a point at a height of 2R from the surface of the Moon which has radius R and mass M. What is the correct expression for the speed of the object on hitting the Moon? A 4 GM 3 R B 2 GM 3 R C 4GM R D 2GM R

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Identify both distances from the Moon’s centre and apply conservation of energy.
questions.misconception: Using height in place of distance from the centre

explanation.body: Conservation of energy gives $E_\mathrm{final}=E_\mathrm{initial}$. The object starts at rest at radius $3R$ and hits the Moon at radius $R$, so $\tfrac12 mv^2-GMm/R=0-GMm/(3R)$. Solving gives $v=\sqrt{4GM/(3R)}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: This loses the factor of two from the kinetic energy term when solving for $v^2$.
perOption.C: This treats the surface gravitational field strength as constant over the entire fall.
perOption.D: This corresponds to starting from rest infinitely far away.

Which graph best shows the variation of the magnitude of force F with distance x from mass M?

Mass M is greater than mass m. d m M x The gravitational force F acting on a third mass mx is measured on a line between the two masses. questions.difficultyReason: Students must infer both the zero of the resultant force and its location.
questions.misconception: Opposing gravitational forces cancel at the midpoint.

explanation.body: At the point where the net force on the third mass is zero, the attractions from $M$ and $m$ are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. Since $M>m$, that point is nearer the smaller mass $m$.

perOption.A: Places the zero near the midpoint, where the larger mass still pulls more strongly.
perOption.B: Keeps the resultant positive throughout the gap, missing the cancellation point.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Places the minimum nearer the smaller mass but leaves a nonzero force there.

questions.stemText:
Two points X and Y are on equipotential lines with potentials $\phi_X$ and $\phi_Y$ which are at distances $3r$ and $r$ respectively from a star. [Two concentric dashed circles are centred on the star. X is on the outer circle labelled $\phi_X$, and Y is on the inner circle labelled $\phi_Y$. Lines from the star to X and Y are labelled $3r$ and $r$.] Which statement is correct?
A The ratio of $\phi_X:\phi_Y$ is $3:1$.
B The ratio of $\phi_X:\phi_Y$ is $9:1$.
C Work done by gravitational field to move a mass from X to Y is positive.
D Work done by external agent to move a mass from Y to X is negative.

stemImage.alt: Question 10: Two points X and Y are on equipotential lines with potentials X and Y which are at distances 3r and r respectively from a star. X 3r X Y r Y Which statement

appearances.originalFile: TMJC/TMJC_2026_H2 Physics_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The student must apply inverse-distance scaling and identify the sign of gravitational work.
questions.misconception: Confusing the distance dependence of potential and field strength

explanation.body: Gravitational potential follows $\phi=-GM/r$, so $\phi_X:\phi_Y=1:3$. Gravitational potential energy decreases from X to Y, so the field does positive work. For the reverse transfer at unchanged kinetic energy, the external agent does positive work.

perOption.A: Reverses the inverse-distance ratio, which is $1:3$.
perOption.B: The potential is inversely proportional to distance, giving $1:3$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: The external agent does positive work when moving the mass from Y to X at unchanged kinetic energy.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Two satellites P and Q are in circular orbits about the Earth. Satellite P has mass m and it is in an orbit of radius r. Satellite Q has mass 2m and it is in an orbit of radius 2r.

Which of the following statements is true?
questions.stemText: Two satellites P and Q are in circular orbits about the Earth. Satellite P has mass m and it is in an orbit of radius r. Satellite Q has mass 2m and it is in an orbit of radius 2r. Q 2r P r Earth Which of the following statements is true? A The speed of satellite Q is greater than that of satellite P. B The speed of satellite Q is the same as that of satellite P. C The kinetic energy of satellite Q is greater than that of satellite P. D The kinetic energy of satellite Q is same as that of satellite P.

options.label: A
options.text: The speed of satellite Q is greater than that of satellite P.

options.label: B
options.text: The speed of satellite Q is the same as that of satellite P.

options.label: C
options.text: The kinetic energy of satellite Q is greater than that of satellite P.

options.label: D
options.text: The kinetic energy of satellite Q is same as that of satellite P.

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The student must derive the orbital speed dependence before comparing kinetic energies.
questions.misconception: Comparing kinetic energies using mass alone.

explanation.body: For a circular orbit of radius $d$, gravity provides the centripetal force, so $GMm/d^2=mv^2/d$. This gives $v=\sqrt{GM/d}$ and $K=\tfrac12mv^2=GMm/(2d)$. Q is slower because its orbit is larger, but doubling both the satellite mass and the orbital radius leaves $K$ equal to $GMm/(2r)$ for each satellite.

perOption.A: Reverses the radius dependence of orbital speed.
perOption.B: Overlooks the dependence of orbital speed on radius.
perOption.C: Counts Q’s greater mass without accounting for its lower speed.
perOption.D: Correct. Both satellites have the same mass-to-orbital-radius ratio.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: Which statement about two satellites of different masses in the geostationary orbit around the Earth is incorrect?
questions.stemText: Which statement about two satellites of different masses in the geostationary orbit around the Earth is incorrect? A The gravitational forces acting on the two satellites are different. B The centripetal acceleration of each satellite is different. C The angular velocities of the two satellites are the same. D The kinetic energy of each satellite is different.

options.label: A
options.text: The gravitational forces acting on the two satellites are different.

options.label: B
options.text: The centripetal acceleration of each satellite is different.

options.label: C
options.text: The angular velocities of the two satellites are the same.

options.label: D
options.text: The kinetic energy of each satellite is different.

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires distinguishing mass-dependent quantities from quantities fixed by the common orbit.
questions.misconception: Confusing gravitational force with gravitational acceleration.

explanation.body: Both satellites are at the same orbital radius, so they experience the same gravitational field strength and hence the same centripetal acceleration. Their gravitational forces differ because $F=mg$ and their masses differ. Their common period of about 24 hours gives the same angular velocity, so $v=r\omega$ gives the same speed, while their different masses give different kinetic energies.

perOption.A: This statement is true because $F=mg$ differs for the two masses at the same field strength.
perOption.B: Correct. Both satellites have the same centripetal acceleration magnitude.
perOption.C: This statement is true because both satellites have the same orbital period.
perOption.D: This statement is true because the satellites have equal speeds and different masses.
